text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Sweden has the lowest rate of fatal traffic accidents in the world, statistics show. In 1996, an estimated 565 people will have been killed with four million cars on the roads.

- As Norway changes its custom laws, Norwegians are expected to buy more goods across the border in Sweden. Norwegians will be allowed to import goods worth 2,000 Norwegian crowns after a day-trip abroad, up from the current 500 crowns. When abroad more than 24 hours, Norwegians will be allowed to purchase items for 5,000 Norwegian crowns, up from 1,200 crowns.

- Internet subscription sellers Telia Telecom and Tele2 were among the winners in the Swedish Christmas shopping spree. While Tele2 had about 100,000 internet customers in November, it has sold 50,000 subscriptions so far in December, according to Helen Lidstrom, head of marketing at Tele2. Telia Telecom did not disclose any figures, but said it won many new customers.

- Swedish high schools use an outdated pedagogy and teachers have problems cooperating, which makes it difficult for many students to get passing grades, according to a report from the parliamentary high school committee, which will be released in January.

- Probability calculations for large accidents with Swedish nuclear power have showed to be completely wrong with risks in some cases being 100 times larger than experts have thought, according to reports from the nuclear power inspectorate SKI.

- 1996 turned out to be record year for the Stockholm Stock Exchange with the exchange's general index ending the year 37 percent higher and turnover increasing by 37 percent to more than 915 billion crowns from 665 billion crowns last year, according to the exchange.

- Sweden's gross national product (GDP) will increase by 3.3 percent in 1997 and 3.1 percent in 1998, forecasts U.S. investment bank Morgan Stanley's Nordic analyst Beshara Madi. Madi is more upbeat than other forecasters. National economic institute KI sees GDP rising 2.7 percent in 1997 and 2.4 percent in 1998. Madi bases his forecasts on an increase in consumer confidence, forecasting the economic upturn will also encompass households and the domestic market, for the first time during the 1990s.

- Next year households will have about the same economic situation as this year, the paper estimates. While real wages will increase, this will to some extent be counterbalanced by higher taxes and lower subsidies.
- A 150 percent boost in clothing retailer Hennes & Mauritz's share during 1996 has made the company one of the ten largest on the Stockholm Stock Exchange.
